lessons.title: Home Sweet Home
objectives: Match animals to their homes
Explain that homes keep animals safe
explanation: Animals need homes to stay safe, rest and raise their babies. Birds build nests in trees. Rabbits dig burrows underground. Bees live in hives.
Fish live in water — in rivers, ponds and the sea. Lions and tigers rest in dens or shady grass.
Some animals live with people: cows and goats on farms, and pets like cats and dogs in our homes.

story.title: The Lost Little Rabbit
story.text: A little rabbit got lost. "Is this my home?" it asked a bird's nest. "Too high!" It peeked into a beehive — "Too buzzy!" It looked in a pond — "Too wet!" At last it found a hole under a bush, and there was Mother Rabbit. "My burrow!" it cried happily.

lessons.title: Caring for Animals
objectives: Describe what pets need
Show safe and kind behaviour with animals
explanation: Like us, animals need food, clean water, shelter and care. Pets also need gentle play and a visit to the vet when they are unwell.
Be gentle: stroke animals softly, never pull tails or ears, and let them rest when they want to.
With street dogs or unknown animals, ask a grown-up first and never put your hand near a strange animal's face. Watch wild animals from a distance — their home is not our playground.

lessons.title: Who Lives Where?
objectives: Name major habitats and their features
Explain why an animal lives in a particular habitat
explanation: A habitat is the natural home of an animal or plant. It gives them food, water, shelter and a place to raise young.

Forests have trees for shelter (tigers, monkeys, hornbills). Deserts are dry and hot or cold (camels, desert foxes). Oceans are salty and deep (whales, octopus). Polar regions are icy (polar bears, penguins — at opposite poles!).
Grasslands are wide and grassy (blackbuck, zebras). Wetlands, like marshes and lakes, attract many birds, including migrating cranes.

vocabulary.meaning: the natural home of a living thing
a wide area covered with grass
land soaked with water, like marshes

examples: Polar bears live in the Arctic; penguins mostly in the Southern Hemisphere.
Flamingos gather in wetlands like the Rann of Kutch.

story.title: The Habitat Swap Party
story.text: At a party, the animals decided to swap homes for a day. The camel went to the ocean — glug! The octopus went to the desert — dry! The polar bear went to the forest — too hot! By evening, everyone rushed home. "My habitat fits me best," they all agreed.

lessons.title: Under the Sea
objectives: Name ocean animals from different groups
Describe coral reefs and why they matter
explanation: Oceans cover about 70% of Earth's surface. They are home to fish, mammals like whales and dolphins, and invertebrates (animals without backbones) like jellyfish, octopus and crabs.

Coral reefs look like rocks but are built by tiny animals called coral polyps. Reefs shelter about a quarter of all ocean species, even though they cover a tiny part of the sea floor. India has reefs in the Gulf of Mannar, Lakshadweep and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
The deep sea is dark and cold. Some deep-sea creatures make their own light — this is called bioluminescence.

vocabulary.meaning: an animal without a backbone
an underwater structure built by tiny coral animals

to do with the sea

examples: A dolphin is a mammal: it breathes air and feeds its baby milk.
An octopus has eight arms and no bones.

story.title: Pala's Reef Tour
story.text: Pala the dolphin gave Kiko a tour of the coral reef. Clownfish peeked from anemones, a turtle munched seagrass, and a shy octopus changed colour to hide. "All of this was built by tiny coral animals," said Pala. "That's why we must keep the sea clean."

lessons.title: Super Senses
objectives: Describe special senses of different animals
Explain echolocation
explanation: Many animals have senses much stronger than ours. Eagles can spot small prey from very high up. Owls see well in dim light and hear tiny rustles.
Dogs have a sense of smell many thousands of times more sensitive than ours, which is why they help find people after disasters.

Bats and dolphins use echolocation: they make sounds and listen for echoes bouncing back, building a "sound picture" of their surroundings. Elephants can communicate using very low rumbles that travel long distances.

vocabulary.meaning: a way of noticing the world (sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch)
finding things by listening to echoes
an animal hunted for food

examples: Snakes "smell" by flicking their tongues.
Elephants may sense rumbles through their feet.

story.text: In total darkness, a little bat swooped between branches. "How do you see?" asked Olu the owl. "I shout!" squeaked the bat. Tiny high-pitched calls bounced off a moth and back to the bat's ears. Snap! Dinner. "I see with sound," said the bat.

lessons.title: Long Journeys
objectives: Explain why animals migrate
Describe hibernation and group behaviour
explanation: Migration is a regular long journey animals make, usually with the seasons, to find food, warmth or places to breed. Amur falcons fly from East Asia, stop in Nagaland in large numbers, then cross the Arabian Sea to Africa — one of the longest bird migrations.

Hibernation is a deep sleep through winter to save energy when food is scarce (some bears and bats). Some animals, like certain frogs and snails, rest through hot dry seasons instead — called aestivation.
Many animals live in groups: elephants in herds led by an older female (the matriarch), wolves in packs, ants and bees in colonies. Groups help find food and protect young.

context.text: Satellite tagging of Amur falcons has tracked journeys of over 20,000 km a year between Asia and southern Africa. Community conservation in Nagaland's Pangti village has protected the roosting falcons since 2013.

vocabulary.meaning: a regular seasonal journey

examples: Flamingos visit Indian wetlands in winter.

story.title: The Village That Protected the Falcons
story.text: Every October, huge flocks of Amur falcons arrive in Nagaland. Years ago, many were hunted. Then the villagers of Pangti decided to protect them. Today, people come from far away to watch the sky fill with falcons, and the village is proud to be their guardian.

lessons.title: India's Iconic Animals
objectives: Locate iconic Indian species and their protected areas
Explain what national parks and wildlife sanctuaries do
explanation: India is one of the world's most biodiverse countries. The Bengal tiger is the national animal. Asiatic lions live in the wild only in Gujarat's Gir forest area. One-horned rhinos thrive in Kaziranga, Assam.
Snow leopards roam the high Himalayas, and Asian elephants live in forests across the south, northeast and the Himalayan foothills.

National parks and wildlife sanctuaries protect habitats by limiting hunting, logging and building. India has two internationally recognised biodiversity hotspots partly within its borders: the Western Ghats and the Himalaya, plus parts of the Indo-Burma and Sundaland hotspots.

story.title: The Last Lions of Asia
story.text: Over a century ago, only a small number of Asiatic lions survived, all in the Gir forest. With protection, the population grew. The 2020 count estimated about 674 lions. "Protection works," said the forest guard, "but all our lions in one region is still a risk."

lessons.title: Saving the Tiger
objectives: Explain the main threats to wildlife
Describe Project Tiger and evaluate its results
explanation: Species become endangered because of habitat loss (forests cleared for farms and roads), poaching (illegal hunting), pollution, invasive species and climate change.

India launched Project Tiger in 1973, creating tiger reserves with protected core areas. Tiger numbers have since increased; the 2022 national estimate was about 3,167 tigers, roughly three-quarters of the world's wild tigers.

The IUCN Red List classifies species by extinction risk: from Least Concern to Critically Endangered, Extinct in the Wild and Extinct. Extinction is forever — like the dodo of Mauritius, extinct since the late 1600s.

context.text: Tiger population estimates come from the All India Tiger Estimation using camera traps and surveys; the 2022 cycle reported a minimum of about 3,167 tigers.

examples: Great Indian Bustard: critically endangered by power lines and habitat loss.

story.text: Before dawn, ranger Meena checked camera traps along the forest trail. One photo showed a tigress with two cubs. She logged it carefully, then patrolled for snares. "Every cub that grows up," she said, "is proof that protection is working."

lessons.title: Scientific Names
objectives: Explain the levels of classification
Use binomial names and dichotomous keys
explanation: Scientists classify living things into nested groups: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. Each level is more specific. Carl Linnaeus developed this system in the 1700s.

Every species has a two-part scientific name (binomial): genus + species, written in italics. The tiger is Panthera tigris; the lion is Panthera leo — both in the genus Panthera, showing they are closely related.
A dichotomous key identifies organisms by a series of yes/no questions: "Does it have legs? → yes → How many? → six → insect."

vocabulary.meaning: sorting living things into groups
a group that can breed to produce fertile offspring
a group of closely related species
a tool using paired choices to identify organisms

examples: Humans: Homo sapiens.
Indian peafowl: Pavo cristatus.

story.title: Why Not Just Call It a Tiger?
story.text: A scientist from Brazil, one from Japan and one from India all studied the same cat — but each language called it something different. Using Panthera tigris, they knew instantly they meant the same animal. "A shared name," they agreed, "is a shared language for science."

lessons.title: Animals Without Backbones
objectives: Describe the main invertebrate groups
Explain the ecological importance of invertebrates
explanation: About 95% or more of animal species are invertebrates — animals without backbones. Arthropods have jointed legs and a hard outer skeleton (exoskeleton): insects (6 legs), arachnids (8 legs: spiders, scorpions) and crustaceans (crabs, prawns).
Molluscs have soft bodies, often with shells (snails, oysters, octopus). Annelids are segmented worms (earthworms). Cnidarians include jellyfish and corals.
Invertebrates do vital jobs: pollinating crops, recycling dead material, aerating soil and feeding birds and fish. Their decline would harm entire ecosystems.

vocabulary.meaning: an animal without a backbone
a hard outer skeleton

examples: Spiders are arachnids, not insects.

story.title: The Tiny Majority
story.text: Professor Hoot asked the class to count every animal in one square metre of garden. They found two birds flying past — and hundreds of ants, beetles, mites, worms and springtails. "The world is run by tiny creatures," Hoot said. "We just don't notice them."

lessons.title: Innate and Learned Behaviour
objectives: Distinguish innate from learned behaviour
Evaluate methods of animal behaviour research
explanation: Innate behaviours are inherited and done without learning — a spider spinning its first web, a baby turtle heading for the sea. Learned behaviours develop through experience — crows learning to use tools, elephants learning migration routes from elders.

Field researchers observe animals in their natural habitats, often for years. Jane Goodall's study of chimpanzees in Tanzania revealed tool use; Salim Ali, "the Birdman of India", conducted systematic bird surveys across India.
Studies of animal cognition show many animals solve problems, remember, and communicate in complex ways — raising questions about how we should treat them.

context.text: Goodall observed chimpanzees making and using termite-fishing tools in 1960. Salim Ali's "The Book of Indian Birds" was first published in 1941.

vocabulary.meaning: inherited, performed without learning
developed through experience
the scientific study of animal behaviour

examples: Weaver birds build complex nests; young males improve with practice.

story.title: The Birdman's Notebook
story.text: As a boy, Salim Ali shot a sparrow with a yellow patch on its throat and took it to the Bombay Natural History Society to ask what it was. That curiosity grew into a lifetime of careful bird surveys across India — and eventually into a powerful voice for protecting birds and their habitats.

lessons.title: Living with Wildlife
objectives: Analyse causes of human–wildlife conflict
Evaluate solutions and ethical positions
explanation: As towns and farms expand into forests, people and wildlife compete for space. Elephants may raid crops; leopards may enter villages at night. Both people and animals can be harmed.

Solutions include wildlife corridors linking forests, early warning systems (SMS alerts when elephants approach), compensation for crop loss, community-based conservation and better land-use planning.

Ethical questions arise: How should we weigh human livelihoods against animal welfare? Should zoos exist? Different philosophies and traditions — including Jain and Buddhist ideas of ahimsa (non-violence) — offer different answers.

context.text: Jainism teaches ahimsa — non-harm — towards all living beings; many Hindus and Buddhists also value non-violence, and some communities, such as the Bishnoi of Rajasthan, protect wildlife as a religious duty.

story.text: In a village at the forest edge, phones buzzed at dusk: "Elephants approaching from the east." Families stayed indoors, and farmers lit lights at field edges as advised. The herd passed through and returned to the forest. No one was hurt — on either side.
